Therefore, concrete placed by free fall usually has a slump of 6 to 7 inches to provide workability, while avoiding segregation, while concrete placed by tremie or pumping usually has a slump of 7 to 9 inches. The concrete must retain workability often for several hours over the duration of placement and retrieval of the casing.
key_points: Rebar cage includes longitudinal bars, transverse hoops/spirals, centering devices, lifting brackets, and tubing for post-grouting and NDT (e.g., cross-hole sonic logging).
AASHTO (2020) requires minimum 6 longitudinal bars (≥ No. 5); steel area ratio typically 1–2%, max 8%; ratios >4% impede concrete flow.
Minimum rebar clear spacing: 5 in. or 5× maximum aggregate size; minimum concrete cover: 3 in. (6 in. for shafts ≥5 ft dia.).
Target 28-day concrete strength: 3,000–5,000 psi; higher strengths used for seismic design.
Free-fall placement: slump 6–7 in.; tremie/pump placement: slump 7–9 in.; concrete must self-consolidate without vibration.
Concrete must resist bleed (water separation) and segregation (paste–aggregate separation) during placement.
Concrete must remain workable for several hours to allow for full placement and casing retrieval.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing and specifying rebar cages and concrete mixes for drilled shaft construction.

sections.title: Post Grouting
sections.summary: Describes post grouting of drilled shaft bases to premobilize and improve base resistance. Explains the mechanism (preloading soil below base, reducing void ratio, grout permeation, enlarged grout bulb), minimum concrete strength required before grouting (>2,500 psi), and the two grout distribution systems: flat jack design and sleeve-port design.
sections.body:
Post grouting is used to premobilize and improve the base resistance in drilled shafts using pressurized grout delivered after the concrete has been placed and allowed to gain sufficient strength (>2500 psi). The premobilizing effect is achieved by loading and compressing the soil below the base. This leads to smaller post-construction settlement needed to mobilize the base resistance under service conditions. The ground improving effect is achieved by reducing the void ratio of the soil below the base, permeating grout into the soil, and/or creating an enlarged grout bulb that effectively increases the base area.

Post grouting requires installing grout delivery tubing and a distribution device to the reinforcement cage prior to placing the cage in the shaft. The grout distribution device can be a flat jack design, where grout is pumped from tubing placed between a steel plate and rubber membrane. Alternatively, grout distribution can use a sleeve-port design, where grout is pumped through multiple U-shaped circuits that contain perforations which are sealed with rubber sleeves. Grout exits the delivery and distribution system when the internal grout pressure exceeds the confinement provided by the rubber sleeve/membrane and pressure from the earth and groundwater.
key_points: Post grouting premobilizes base resistance by preloading and compressing soil below the shaft base, reducing settlement needed to mobilize base resistance under service loads.
Ground improvement mechanisms: void ratio reduction, grout permeation into soil, and/or formation of an enlarged grout bulb that increases effective base area.
Grouting is performed after concrete has cured to >2,500 psi compressive strength.
Grout delivery tubing and distribution device must be attached to the rebar cage before it is placed in the shaft.
Flat jack design: grout pumped between a steel plate and rubber membrane.
Sleeve-port design: grout pumped through U-shaped circuits with rubber-sleeve-sealed perforations; grout exits when internal pressure exceeds earth/groundwater confinement.
sections.applicability: Applies when post grouting is specified to enhance base resistance and reduce settlement in drilled shaft foundations.

sections.title: Continuous-Flight Auger Piles
sections.summary: Covers the construction method, equipment, dimensional ranges, installation constraints, and quality control considerations for continuous-flight auger (CFA) piles (auger cast-in-place piles). Describes the drilling, grouting, and reinforcement sequence, key differences from drilled shafts, site applicability, and the critical balance of rotation vs. penetration rate during drilling.
sections.body:
Continuous-flight auger (CFA) piles, or auger cast-in-place piles, are similar to drilled shafts in that they are bored piles. However, there are a number of significant differences. First, the hole is drilled in one continuous operation and is always supported by augers, which eliminates need for slurry and/or casing. Second, grout or concrete is pumped under pressure through the augers as they are withdrawn. Third, steel reinforcement is pushed into the uncured grout or concrete pile after the augers are withdrawn. The reinforcement commonly extends through only the upper portion of the pile that is subjected to bending.

CFAs are installed with rotary drill rigs typically to depths up to 100 ft using augers that have a diameter ranging from 12 to 36 inches. With the proper equipment, CFAs can be constructed in low headroom conditions and at a batter angle. CFAs can be installed in soil and some weak/weathered rock but cannot be used in hard rock like drilled shafts. CFAs are also not recommended in geologic formations containing voids. A key to good construction quality is balancing the rotation and penetration rate of the augers so that the augers do not excessively rotate and mine soil from beyond the intended limits of the pile. During drilling, the excavated cuttings should ideally be limited to the volume occupied by the auger plus some accommodation for bulking of the disturbed material. This objective can be difficult to achieve in soft clays that tend to squeeze inward and loose clean sands and gravels prone to caving.

After drilling, grout or concrete is pumped at pressure that exceeds the overburden pressure at the bottom of the auger. As grout is pumped, the auger is withdrawn at a rate that compensates for the volume of grout delivered. As the augers are withdrawn, they are either not rotated or rotated slowly in the direction of drilling.
key_points: CFA piles are bored piles drilled in one continuous operation; augers provide continuous hole support, eliminating the need for slurry or casing.
Grout or concrete is pumped under pressure (exceeding overburden pressure at auger tip) through the hollow auger stem as the auger is withdrawn.
Steel reinforcement is pushed into uncured grout/concrete after auger withdrawal and typically extends only through the upper bending zone of the pile.
Typical installation depth is up to 100 ft with auger diameters from 12 to 36 inches using rotary drill rigs; batter angles and low headroom installations are possible.
CFAs are suitable in soil and weak/weathered rock but NOT in hard rock or formations containing voids.
Construction quality control requires balancing auger rotation and penetration rate to prevent over-mining of soil; soft clays and loose clean sands/gravels are particularly challenging.
Withdrawal rate of the auger must compensate for the volume of grout delivered to maintain pile integrity.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or specifying continuous-flight auger (auger cast-in-place) piles in soil or weak/weathered rock conditions.

sections.title: Drilled Displacement Piles
sections.summary: Covers drilled displacement piles (DDPs), which use special soil-displacing augers (e.g., DeWaal, Omega) rather than conventional continuous flight augers. Discusses auger variants, the amelioration process, and key trade-offs vs. CFAs including lateral stress, side resistance, torque requirements, and risks of ground heave in soft soils.
sections.body:
Drilled displacement piles (DDPs) are similar to CFAs in that a continuous operation is used to drill on the downstroke and pump grout or concrete on the upstroke. Instead of the conventional continuous flight augers used by CFAs, DDPs use special augers that displace soil laterally during drilling. Many variants of the augers, e.g., DeWaal and Omega, can be used to drill DDPs, some of which are proprietary. The primary differences among the augers are the amount of displacement (full or partial), the ability to install reinforcement through a hollow stem prior to grouting, and the shaping of the sides of the hole, e.g., smooth or screw-shaped, as the auger is withdrawn during grouting. Some augers use a sacrificial tip that is left in the hole as the grout or concrete is placed when the auger is withdrawn. In some cases, a process known as amelioration, in which sand or gravel is added to the top of the drill hole, is performed to increase shaft resistance.

One advantage of DDPs over CFAs includes the possibility of greater lateral stress between the pile and the soil under certain ground conditions. The side resistances approach those of driven displacement piles. From the standpoint of constructability, DDPs require less finesse by the operator to balance the rate of rotation and the rate of penetration compared to CFAs. DDPs require greater torque to turn the soil-displacing bit, which is a disadvantage compared to CFAs. They also have greater potential for ground heave and/or lateral squeeze of soft soils due to the volume displaced by the pile.
key_points: DDPs use soil-displacing augers (e.g., DeWaal, Omega) rather than conventional CFA augers, displacing soil laterally during drilling.
Auger variants differ in displacement amount (full or partial), ability to install rebar through a hollow stem, and hole-wall shaping (smooth vs. screw-shaped).
Amelioration — adding sand or gravel to the top of the drill hole — can be used to increase shaft resistance.
DDPs can achieve greater lateral stress and side resistances approaching those of driven displacement piles.
DDPs require less operator finesse than CFAs but demand greater torque for the soil-displacing bit.
Greater potential for ground heave and lateral squeeze of soft soils is a key disadvantage of DDPs vs. CFAs.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or specifying drilled displacement piles (DDPs) as an alternative to CFA piles, particularly in competent soils where high side resistance is needed.

sections.title: Aggregate Columns
sections.summary: Introduces aggregate columns, including rammed aggregate piers and stone columns, as a deep foundation type (Z/b ≥ 5). Describes two construction methods — vibro-replacement (wet stone columns using a down-hole vibrator and water jet) and vibro-displacement — and notes that stone columns up to 100 ft in length are achievable.
sections.body:
Aggregate columns include rammed aggregate piers and stone columns (see Figure 1-2). Aggregate columns are not usually structurally-connected to the superstructure, but they often provide the function of a foundation and meet the definition of a deep foundation (Z/b ≥ 5) adopted herein. Stone columns up to 100 ft in length can be formed using either vibro-replacement or vibro-displacement.

Vibro-replacement columns, a.k.a wet stone columns, are constructed using a down-hole vibrator and water jet to penetrate the ground. The hole is filled with stone dumped [text continues beyond chunk].
key_points: Aggregate columns encompass rammed aggregate piers and stone columns; they typically are not structurally connected to the superstructure.
They qualify as deep foundations under the Z/b ≥ 5 criterion adopted in this UFC.
Stone columns up to 100 ft in length can be formed by either vibro-replacement or vibro-displacement methods.
Vibro-replacement (wet stone columns) uses a down-hole vibrator and water jet to penetrate the ground, with the hole then filled with stone.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or selecting aggregate column ground improvement systems (rammed aggregate piers or stone columns) as deep foundation elements.

sections.title: Micropiles
sections.summary: Covers the design, construction, and installation of micropiles — small-diameter (<12 in), grouted deep foundation elements suitable for difficult access, low headroom, and challenging ground conditions. Topics include drilling equipment and techniques, grout types and delivery methods (Types A–D per FHWA 2005), bond zone characteristics, reinforcement details, and pile-to-cap connection options.
sections.body:
Micropiles are bored with a small diameter (<12 inches) and grouted with foundation elements that can be installed in soil and rock to depths up to 200 ft. Greater depths can be achieved with special equipment. Micropiles are very adaptable to drilling in low headroom conditions, hard to access sites, challenging ground conditions, and in close proximity to existing facilities. Micropiles can also readily be installed at a batter angle. Figure 6-10 shows one example of a micropile construction sequence. However, there are many variations to the construction process particularly related to the drilling technique, casing, drilling fluid, grout delivery technique, and number of grouting phases.

Micropile drill rigs are usually mounted on trucks or tracked equipment. Drill rigs usually incorporate a hydraulic power unit to rotate the casing and/or drill rod in the same or opposite directions. Drilling tools are selected to be compatible with the ground conditions and include roller bits, casing with cutter teeth, rock bits, augers, and percussive hammers. Percussive tools, primarily used for rock drilling, may be powered by the rig's hydraulic power unit or a separate air compressor. Percussive force is applied using either a top-drive hammer or down-the-hole hammer. Sonic drilling advances the hole by vibrating the casing and drill rod. The drill hole is usually flushed by water or slurry to remove cuttings, stabilize the hole when casing is not used, and cool drill bits. Compressed air can also be used to flush the hole but should not be used below the groundwater table, especially in sands. Drilling fluids present the need to supply and circulate the fluid as well as manage spoils.

Micropiles are grouted to create a bond zone with the surrounding soil or rock. Bond zone lengths of 5 to 10 ft are common in rock while longer bond lengths are routinely used in soil. The diameter of the bond zone is influenced by the inside diameter of casing that is used, the use of an underreaming bit to enlarge the drill hole below the casing, and the method of grouting. The grout used for micropile construction is most often a neat cement prepared using a water cement ratio of about 0.40–0.50 by weight to achieve typical target compressive strengths of 4,000 to 5,000 psi. As defined by FHWA (2005), Type A micropiles are grouted under gravity only, while Type B micropiles are first gravity grouted and additional grout is added under pressure as the casing is withdrawn. Type C micropiles are first gravity grouted then post grouted under pressure prior to hardening of the initial grout. Type D micropiles are first gravity grouted and then post grouted under pressure one or more times after hardening of the initial grout. The post grouting for Type C and D micropiles does not occur concurrently with removal of casing. Generally, Type A micropiles are used when the bond zone is in stiff clay or rock while Type B, C, and D micropiles are used in soils.

Micropiles are typically reinforced by a steel pipe and/or a centralized steel rebar that carries at least 40% of the load in the element. The casing is often an 80 ksi steel oil field casing (API N-80) with an outside diameter of 5.5, 7.0, or 9.625 inches and approximately a half-inch wall thickness. The rebar is often a large diameter thread bar, e.g., #18 or #20, made from 75 or 80 ksi steel.

Micropiles are commonly installed in groups and tied together within a pile cap. There are a variety of options available for establishing the connection between the micropile and the pile cap that depend on whether the pile cap (or footing) is new or existing and how heavily the pile is loaded in compression, tension, and bending. For example, the inset in Figure 6-10 shows a pile to cap connection for a pile subjected to significant loads in compression, tension, and bending. One or both of the bearing plates and stiffeners may be omitted if not needed.

Note: Typically mill secondary pipe is used because prime pipe is very expensive. Use of mill secondary pipe requires the implementation of coupon tests, typically two per truckload of pipe, because mill certifications are not available for this material.
key_points: Micropiles are small-diameter (<12 in) grouted elements installable to depths up to 200 ft in soil and rock, adaptable to low headroom, difficult access, and battered installation.
Drilling tools include roller bits, rock bits, augers, and percussive hammers; sonic drilling advances the hole by vibrating casing and drill rod.
Hole flushing uses water or slurry; compressed air should NOT be used below the groundwater table, especially in sands.
Bond zones are 5–10 ft in rock (longer in soil); grout is neat cement at w/c ratio 0.40–0.50 targeting 4,000–5,000 psi compressive strength.

FHWA (2005) defines four micropile types (A–D) based on grouting method: Type A = gravity only; Type B = gravity + pressure during casing withdrawal; Types C & D = post-grouted after initial grout placement.
Reinforcement requires steel pipe and/or centrally placed rebar carrying ≥40% of element load; typical casing is API N-80 (80 ksi) at 5.5, 7.0, or 9.625 in OD with ~0.5 in wall.
Micropiles are grouped and connected to pile caps; connection detail varies by whether cap is new or existing and by compression, tension, and bending demand.
figures: Figure 6-10 Micropiles – (a) Construction Sequence and (b) Connection Detail
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or specifying micropile foundations for new or retrofit construction, particularly in constrained sites, challenging ground, or where deep load transfer to rock or competent soil is required.

sections.title: Helical Piles
sections.summary: Describes helical (screw) piles: their construction from helical steel bearing plates welded to a central shaft, typical dimensions (helix diameters 6–36 in, lengths 10–30 ft), installation methods using hydraulic rotary drills, suitability for tension and compression loads, use of installation torque for capacity evaluation, corrosion protection via galvanizing, and limitations in hard or gravelly soils.
sections.body:
Helical piles, or screw piles, consist of one or more circular steel bearing plates that are formed into a helix shape with a uniform pitch and welded to a central round or square steel shaft. The pitch of the helix is shaped so that the shaft advances the pitch distance in one revolution without excessive soil disturbance. When properly installed, helical piles are low-displacement elements. Typical helix diameters range from 6 to 36 inches, and completed helical piles lengths are mostly 10 to 30 ft; however, greater depths are routinely obtained using larger piles and equipment. Helical piles are usually installed in segments that are connected using bolted couplings. Since helical piles usually involve steel in direct contact with the ground, the components are galvanized to resist corrosion. Many specifications require a minimum embedment depth of five or more times the largest helix diameter between the ground surface and the upper-most helix. Generally, there are no more than 6 helices per pile. Helical piles are not suitable for ground conditions that may damage the shaft or helices, such as hard soils or soils with large gravel or cobbles. Specialty helical piles are grouted along the shaft to increase the strength and stiffness of the pile as well as increase resistance to buckling and corrosion.

Helical piles are installed using hydraulically-powered rotary drills that are often small enough to be mounted on a light tracked loader/excavator or a truck. Helical piles are very adaptable to installation in low headroom conditions, hard to access sites, and in close proximity to existing facilities. Helical piles can readily be installed at a batter angle with proper equipment and can be used for resisting tension loads as well as compressive loads. The installation torque is an important parameter to evaluate capacity and is often measured in the field using a variety of qualitative or quantitative torque indicators. These methods include 1) observing the amount of twist in the shaft over some shaft length (qualitative), 2) using torque-limiting shear pins (quantitative at points of pin failure), 3) digital torque indicators (continuous quantitative readings using strain measurements), and 4) differential pressure torque indicators (continuous quantitative readings using the pressure drop through the hydraulic drill).
key_points: Helical piles consist of one or more helical steel bearing plates welded to a round or square central shaft; they are low-displacement elements when properly installed.
Typical helix diameters range from 6 to 36 inches; pile lengths are mostly 10–30 ft, with no more than 6 helices per pile.
Minimum embedment depth is commonly specified as five or more times the largest helix diameter above the uppermost helix.
Not suitable for hard soils or soils with large gravel/cobbles that could damage the shaft or helices.
Can resist both tension and compressive loads and can be installed at a batter angle.
Installation torque is a key capacity indicator, measured qualitatively or quantitatively via shaft twist, shear pins, digital strain gauges, or hydraulic pressure drop.
Steel components are galvanized for corrosion resistance; specialty versions are grouted along the shaft for added strength, stiffness, and buckling resistance.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating, specifying, or installing helical (screw) piles for deep foundation applications, especially in low-headroom, restricted-access, or tension-load scenarios.

sections.title: Geotechnical Static Axial Capacity and Settlement
sections.summary: Top-level container section covering analysis methods for evaluating the static axial capacity and settlement of deep foundations. References Section 6-8 for static load testing and Section 6-9 for dynamic methods, which refine initial performance estimates. All detailed content is in the subsections below.
key_points: This section presents selected analysis methods for static axial capacity and settlement of deep foundations.
Section 6-8 covers static load testing; Section 6-9 covers dynamic methods — both provide important refinements to initial capacity estimates.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or analyzing deep foundations where static axial capacity and settlement must be evaluated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the scope of Section 6-5, which presents selected analysis methods for evaluating static axial capacity and settlement of deep foundations. Notes that static load testing (Section 6-8) and dynamic methods (Section 6-9) provide important refinements to initial performance estimates derived from the analysis methods covered here.
sections.body: This section presents selected analysis methods for evaluating static axial capacity and settlement of deep foundations. Section 6-8 describes static load testing, and Section 6-9 describes dynamic methods, which provide important refinements to the initial estimates of the anticipated performance of the deep foundations.
key_points: Section 6-5 covers selected analysis methods for static axial capacity and settlement of deep foundations.
Static load testing (Section 6-8) and dynamic methods (Section 6-9) refine initial capacity and performance estimates produced by the analysis methods in this section.
sections.applicability: Applies at the start of any deep foundation analysis where static axial capacity and settlement need to be estimated and subsequently verified by load testing.

sections.title: Limit States
sections.summary: Container section covering the strength and service limit states for deep foundation design under both LRFD and ASD frameworks. Defines how nominal resistance is reduced (via resistance factors or factors of safety) and specifies the acceptable deformation limits that govern service life performance.
key_points: Two primary limit states govern deep foundation design: strength (capacity) and service (deformation).
LRFD uses resistance factors to reduce nominal resistance; ASD uses a factor of safety to derive allowable/working values.
Extreme Event Limit State (AASHTO 2020) addresses survivability under collisions, blasts, earthquakes, scour, and liquefaction but is outside the scope of this manual.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and applying a design framework (LRFD or ASD) for deep foundation elements subject to compressive or uplift loading.

sections.title: Strength Limit State
sections.summary: Defines the strength limit state for deep foundations as the extent to which nominal resistance can be mobilized over the service life. Covers differences in resistance factoring between shaft and base components, uncertainty in capacity prediction methods, and criteria for interpreting load test results using methods such as Davisson (1972).
sections.body:
Static capacity analyses are performed to estimate the nominal resistance (LRFD) or the ultimate capacity (ASD) of a foundation element subjected to compressive or uplift loading. The nominal resistance or ultimate capacity of a foundation element is evaluated by considering the geotechnical strength of the geomaterials and the structural strength of the material(s) that comprise the foundation element. The strength limit state is defined by the extent to which the nominal resistance may be mobilized under the expected conditions over the service life of the foundation. In the LRFD framework, the nominal resistance is reduced by application of resistance factors. In the ASD framework, an allowable (working) value is determined using a factor of safety. In some cases, different factors are applied to the resistances provided by shaft and base. For example, drilled shafts require greater vertical deformation to mobilize base resistance and have greater uncertainty associated with bearing capacity predictions. Thus, the base resistance is assigned a lower resistance factor.

Often, the criteria defining nominal resistance used to develop static capacity analysis methods are not well documented (Fellenius 2021). While this shortcoming may not be significant in routine design, it is worth referring to original sources, particularly on projects with small allowances for settlement. As discussed in Section 6-8, methods such as the Davisson (1972) failure criterion can be applied to interpret load test results to define nominal resistance in a consistent way.

AASHTO (2020) also defines the Extreme Event Limit State, which is a special case of the strength limit state in which survivability rather than satisfactory performance is the intent of the design checks. Examples of extreme events include loads from collisions, blasts, and earthquakes as well as the impacts of scour from severe flooding and liquefaction. Generally, not all extreme event scenarios are assumed to occur simultaneously in design. Consideration of extreme events is outside the scope of this manual.
key_points: Nominal resistance is evaluated from both geotechnical strength of geomaterials and structural strength of the foundation element.
LRFD applies resistance factors; ASD applies a factor of safety — different factors may apply to shaft vs. base resistance.
Drilled shaft base resistance receives a lower resistance factor due to greater deformation needed for mobilization and higher prediction uncertainty.
Davisson (1972) failure criterion provides a consistent method to interpret load test results and define nominal resistance.
Extreme Event Limit State (survivability under extreme loads/scour/liquefaction) is defined by AASHTO 2020 but is outside the scope of this manual.
sections.applicability: Applies during static capacity analysis of deep foundation elements under compressive or uplift loading using either LRFD or ASD design frameworks.

sections.title: Service Limit State
sections.summary: Defines the service limit state for deep foundations as the acceptable limits on deformation — including settlement and lateral deflection — over the foundation's service life. References Section 6-5.8 for typical settlement limits and Section 6-6.2 for lateral deflection limits.
sections.body: The service limit state is defined by the acceptable limits on deformation, e.g., settlement and lateral deflection, over the service life of the foundation. Section 6-5.8 describes some typical limits for settlement and Section 6-6.2 for lateral deflection.
key_points: Service limit state governs when deformation — settlement or lateral deflection — is the controlling design criterion.
Typical settlement limits are discussed in Section 6-5.8; lateral deflection limits in Section 6-6.2.
Both settlement and lateral deflection must remain within acceptable bounds over the full service life of the foundation.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating deep foundation designs against deformation (settlement and lateral deflection) performance criteria over the service life.

sections.title: Load Transfer
sections.summary: Covers the mechanics of axial load transfer in deep foundations, including shaft and base resistance mobilization, displacement requirements, the effect of relative movement direction, negative skin friction, and the equations for computing nominal shaft and base resistances. Includes discussion of practical reductions (e.g., 80% reduction in drilled shaft base resistance) and factors influencing the factoring of resistances to LRFD or ASD values.
sections.body:
The nominal axial resistance in a deep foundation element, R, is developed from shaft resistance, Rs, and/or base resistance, Rb. The contribution of each source of resistance depends upon the mobilization of shear strength at the soil-shaft or rock-shaft interface and the soil or rock at the base. The peak and post-peak strength is influenced by the usual compositional and environmental factors that govern soil behavior with respect to strength. Of particular note is the differential shear movement between the soil and shaft as well as the movement of the base required to mobilize shaft and base resistances. Normally, full mobilization of shaft resistance occurs within a ½ inch of column top settlement (FHWA 2018a); however, mobilization of the base typically requires larger column settlements. Full base mobilization in fine-grained soils may require column settlement of about 4% to 5% of the base, width, or diameter while settlements of about 10% of the base, width, or diameter may be required for columns in coarse-grained soils (FHWA 2018a). Full mobilization of shaft and base resistance usually do not occur simultaneously. For large elements, such as drilled shafts, the settlements required to fully mobilize the base may exceed the service limit state criteria. Post-grouting of drilled shafts, described in Section 6-4.2.3, can be implemented to reduce the settlement needed to mobilize the base resistance. A useful rule of thumb to evaluate the nominal base resistance of drilled shafts without post grouting that considers the displacement required for mobilization of resistance at working loads is to reduce the nominal base resistance by 80%, i.e., use a nominal base resistance equal to 20% of the full value as evaluated by static capacity analysis or load testing (Gregory 2023). Application of this rule of thumb still requires that a factor of safety or LRFD resistance factor be applied to the reduced nominal base resistance. This rule was developed for shafts bearing in sedimentary rock and hard clays, but is considered to be generally applicable to shafts bearing on rock as well as competent clays, sands, and gravels.

Figure 6-11 illustrates the basic concepts of load transfer. Inset (a) shows the case of an end bearing pile where the soil along the shaft is too weak to consider in design, or the bearing stratum is so stiff that the expected displacements are insufficient to mobilize shaft resistance. Inset (b) shows a case that could represent a friction pile in uniform clay that provides uniform unit shaft resistance in the short term with a small contribution of base resistance, i.e., the ratio of Rb/R is small. Inset (c) shows a case that could represent a pile in uniform, coarse-grained soil that provides unit shaft resistance that is proportional to the effective vertical stress and a large contribution of base resistance, i.e., the ratio of Rb/R is large.

Figure 6-11 also shows two hypothetical relationships between axial load applied to the top of the pile and the resulting settlement. When Rb/R is small, the resistance is primarily from the shaft, which mobilizes at small displacements. The condition of plunge is associated with a significant increase in the rate of settlement with respect to additional loading. This results in a large increase in the slope of the curve when load is applied to a pile where shaft resistance is already fully mobilized. When Rb/R is large, the resistance is primarily from the base, which mobilizes at larger displacements. While the rate of settlement with respect to additional loading may increase as the full mobilization of base resistance approaches, plunge usually does not occur if the bearing stratum is coarse-grained soil, stiff clay, or rock. Therefore, as mentioned in Section 6-5.4, the interpretation of the nominal resistance is not always straightforward. In particular, the nominal base resistance is usually estimated by analytical methods developed from load test data where failure requires interpretation by the Davisson or other failure criterion.

It is also important to consider that the direction of the displacement of the foundation relative to the soil or rock determines whether load is transferred to or from the element to the soil or rock. Base resistance requires that the foundation element moves downward relative to the bearing stratum. Shaft resistance, i.e., load transferred from the element to the bearing stratum, in compression requires that the foundation element moves downward relative to the surrounding material. Mobilization of uplift resistance along the element shaft requires upward movement of the element relative to the surrounding material (see Section 6-5.6). Relative upward movement of the base does not contribute to uplift resistance by mobilizing shear strength. However, short term resistance can be generated by a suction effect if the rate at which the element moves produces negative excess pore water pressures by exceeding the rate of drainage (Bowles 1996). This suction effect is transient and should not be relied upon in design unless the element is specifically designed to utilize it, as with suction caissons used in offshore applications. A condition known as negative skin friction, where load is transferred from the soil to the element, occurs when the soil moves down relative to the element, for example, from consolidation, secondary compression, or vibration-induced densification. Negative skin friction is discussed in Section 6-5.7.

The nominal resistance, R, is the sum of the nominal shaft resistance, Rs, and base resistance, Rb:

R = Rs + Rb   (6-3).

The nominal shaft resistance is computed by multiplying the unit shaft resistance by the surface area. For heterogenous ground conditions, the shaft can be discretized into multiple segments (i) in which each can be represented by a constant unit shaft resistance and the nominal shaft resistance is:

Rs = Σ(fs,i · As,i)   (6-4)

where:
fs,i = unit shaft resistance for segment i and
As,i = surface area for segment i.

Figure 6-12(a) shows important dimensions for deep foundation elements in sand and clay profiles. In cases where the base of the element is enlarged, it is important to distinguish the diameter used to evaluate the surface area of the shaft, B′, versus the diameter used to evaluate the area of the base, B. Figure 6-12 also shows that it is common practice to exclude the upper 5 ft of side resistance, or to the depth of seasonal moisture change or frost depth. This exclusion accounts for the potential for softening and/or gapping of the ground leading to a loss or unexpected reduction of shaft resistance (FHWA 2018a). The potential of softening and/or gaps developing from low confining stress and/or volumetric changes in the soil due to changes in temperature or moisture should be evaluated based on local experience and engineering judgment.

The nominal base resistance is computed by multiplying the unit base resistance, qb, by the appropriate surface area of the base, Ab, as:

Rb = qb · Ab   (6-5).

For formed-in-place columns and driven high-displacement piles, the appropriate base area is the full cross-sectional area as illustrated in Figure 6-12(b). For driven low-displacement piles, the appropriate base area is the area of the pile material. In some situations where a soil plug forms, the decision of how to calculate base area may not be obvious.

The factoring of the nominal shaft and base resistances to reduced (LRFD) or allowable values (ASD) of shaft resistance and base resistance is often dictated by agency practices or code requirements but may be additionally influenced by:
• Consideration of uncertainty in material properties (variable deposits, weak soils such as soft clay and organics)
• Events that have the potential to occur during the service life of the foundation (scour, seasonal shrink/swell, volume change from temperature or geothermal energy foundations, formation of voids in karst, vibration, liquefaction, impacts of future construction/excavation/loading)
• Costs of a more conservative design
• Consequences of unsatisfactory performance.

In some cases, the consequences of uncertain conditions and/or events can be modeled by analytical or numerical analysis, or observed by testing during construction using load testing. However, the actual consequences cannot be precisely known. Therefore, the tools of foundation design have embedded conservatism that, along with engineering judgement, are intended to produce reliable designs. Designers can take efforts to reduce uncertainty through a more robust geotechnical exploration and testing program, performance testing foundation elements via load tests, and working with the entire design team to better estimate the loads applied to the foundation.
key_points: Full mobilization of shaft resistance typically occurs within ½ inch of column top settlement; base mobilization requires 4–5% of base diameter in fine-grained and ~10% in coarse-grained soils (FHWA 2018a).
Shaft and base resistance are generally not fully mobilized simultaneously — for large drilled shafts, full base mobilization may exceed service limit state criteria.

Rule of thumb for drilled shafts without post-grouting: reduce nominal base resistance by 80% (use 20% of full value) at working loads; resistance factor or factor of safety still applies to the reduced value.
Nominal resistance R = Rs + Rb (Eq. 6-3); shaft resistance computed by summing unit resistance × area over discrete segments (Eq. 6-4); base resistance = unit base resistance × base area (Eq. 6-5).
Upper 5 ft of shaft resistance (or to depth of seasonal moisture change/frost depth) is commonly excluded to account for potential softening or gapping.
Negative skin friction transfers load FROM soil TO the element when soil settles relative to the element (e.g., from consolidation or vibration densification).
Suction resistance at the base during uplift is transient and should not be relied upon in design except for elements specifically designed for it (e.g., suction caissons).
Resistance factoring is influenced by material uncertainty, service-life events (scour, liquefaction, karst, etc.), cost of conservatism, and consequences of failure.

equations.description: Nominal resistance R equals the sum of nominal shaft resistance Rs and base resistance Rb: R = Rs + Rb
Nominal shaft resistance computed by summing the product of unit shaft resistance fs,i and surface area As,i over all shaft segments i: Rs = Σ(fs,i · As,i)
Nominal base resistance equals unit base resistance qb multiplied by base area Ab: Rb = qb · Ab

sections.title: Limits on Unit Resistances
sections.summary: Discusses empirical limits on unit shaft and base resistances in static capacity analysis methods, focusing on coarse-grained soils. Covers the concept of critical depth (USACE 1991), maximum unit resistance caps (API 2011), and the debate over whether these limits are technically justified, with specific depth multipliers for loose and dense sands.
sections.body:
Static capacity analysis methods that are at least partially based on empirical observations from load tests may include limits on unit base and shaft resistances. These limits prevent extrapolation of relationships between unit capacity and the input(s) beyond those originally observed by the developers. Such limits may be revised based on site-specific information and engineering judgment.

For coarse-grained soils, some design guidance defines a critical depth (USACE 1991) beyond which the unit shaft and base resistances of foundations no longer increase with additional penetration. Other guidance caps the maximum unit resistance based on soil type and relative density (API 2011). The concepts of critical depth and maximum unit resistance are disputed (Fellenius 2021). USACE (1991) recommends limiting unit shaft and base resistances to the value at a depth of 10·b for loose sands and 20·b for dense sands. API (2011) recommends limiting unit shaft and base resistances as the [text continues].
key_points: Empirical limits on unit shaft and base resistances prevent extrapolation of capacity relationships beyond the range of original observations.
USACE (1991) defines a 'critical depth' beyond which unit shaft and base resistance no longer increase: limit at depth 10·b for loose sands and 20·b for dense sands.
API (2011) caps maximum unit resistances based on soil type and relative density.
The concepts of critical depth and maximum unit resistance are technically disputed (Fellenius 2021).
Limits may be revised based on site-specific data and engineering judgment.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing static capacity analysis of deep foundations in coarse-grained soils where empirical unit resistance limits or critical depth concepts are invoked per USACE 1991 or API 2011 guidance.

sections.title: Static Axial Capacity in Compression for Single Elements
sections.summary: Introduces the four common methods for evaluating geotechnical resistance of deep foundations in compression: Static Capacity Analysis (SCA), numerical analysis, dynamic methods, and load testing. Explains the role of Beta and Alpha SCA methods, their semi-empirical basis, and provides LRFD resistance factors (Table 6-11) and ASD factors of safety (Table 6-12) for driven piles, drilled shafts, and micropiles.
sections.body:
As stated in Section 6-5.2.1, the factored axial resistance of a deep foundation element is determined by the lesser of the factored structural resistance and the factored resistance provided by the soil and/or rock, which is often referred to as the factored geotechnical resistance. Usually, the geotechnical resistance controls design. Common methods used in practice to evaluate the geotechnical resistance are:
1) Static Capacity Analysis (SCA),
2) Numerical analysis,
3) Dynamic methods, e.g., Wave Equation (WE), dynamic measurements, signal matching, and
4) Trial installation and load testing, e.g., test piles.

As described in Section 6-2.1, the normal process of deep foundation design follows a path of making initial estimates of performance using simple analytical models that are iteratively refined using more sophisticated analyses. In many cases, test pile programs are used to calibrate the analytical models. Load testing and dynamic methods, such as signal matching, are often used to update the design, which is an application of the observational method that is the hallmark of sound decision making in geotechnical engineering.

The Static Capacity Analysis (SCA) methods presented herein should be viewed as a step toward a complete foundation design. In addition to providing an estimate of capacity with relatively little effort and no specialty equipment or software, these simple methods provide a rational means to provide inputs for more sophisticated analyses to estimate capacity and/or assess driveability. In general, the predictive accuracy of SCA methods is low (Jardine et al 2001), and it is usually not clear what criteria was used to define the nominal axial capacity (Fellenius 2021).

While there are many SCA methods for driven piles and formed-in-place columns, only the Beta method for effective stress analysis of capacity and the Alpha method for total stress analysis of capacity are presented here. These methods were selected because there is widespread familiarity with these methods in US practice. In addition, there are versions for both driven pile and formed-in-place columns, and the methods are easy to implement. For continuity with historical tradition, the Beta method is categorized as being applicable to coarse-grained soils while the Alpha method is categorized as being applicable to fine-grained soils. In addition to coarse-grained soils, the Beta method is applicable to any soil in a drained condition, e.g., long-term analysis of capacity in clay soils. The Alpha method is targeted at clay soils and some silts that are routinely represented by the undrained condition in the short term. The Beta and Alpha methods are semi-empirical, meaning that they have been calibrated to load test results. For this reason, the guidance presented herein does not encompass all possible ground conditions.

Drilled displacement piles have not yet reached a state of maturity where specific versions of the Beta and Alpha method are available; however, guidance using results from the SPT and CPT are presented in Section 6-5.4.4. According to Coduto et al. (2016), full-displacement DDPs will have shaft resistance that is at least as high as driven piles and base resistance that is on par with CFAs. Therefore, guidance for estimating the shaft resistance of concrete driven piles and the base resistance of CFAs can be used for full-displacement DDPs. For partial-displacement DDPs that generate some spoils, the shaft resistance is between full-displacement DDPs and CFAs (Coduto et al. 2016).

The design methods for aggregate columns and helical piles are significantly different from driven piles and drilled columns. Design guidance for aggregate columns can be found in FHWA (2017), and guidance for helical piles is provided in Perko (2009).

When using an LRFD framework, AASHTO (2020) recommends the resistance factors provided in Table 6-11. Note that resistance factors have not yet been calibrated by AASHTO for certain analysis methods, e.g., Beta Method for driven piles and deep foundation technologies other than driven piles, drilled shafts, and micropiles. For the extreme limit state, a resistance factor equal to 1.0 can be used for compressive axial loading.

Table 6-12 provides recommended minimum factors of safety for loading in compression when allowable stress design is used.
key_points: Geotechnical resistance typically governs deep foundation design over structural resistance.
Four methods for evaluating geotechnical resistance: SCA, numerical analysis, dynamic methods, and load testing.
Beta method (effective stress) applies to coarse-grained soils and drained conditions; Alpha method (total stress) applies to fine-grained, undrained soils.
SCA methods are semi-empirical and have low predictive accuracy; they serve as initial estimates and inputs to more refined analyses.
For full-displacement DDPs, use driven concrete pile shaft resistance and CFA base resistance guidance; for partial-displacement DDPs, interpolate between the two.
LRFD resistance factors per AASHTO (2020) provided in Table 6-11; ASD minimum factors of safety in Table 6-12.
For the extreme limit state, a resistance factor of 1.0 may be used for compressive axial loading.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and applying Static Capacity Analysis methods for single deep foundation elements loaded in compression, under either LRFD or ASD design frameworks.

sections.title: Shaft Resistance in Drained Conditions – Beta Method
sections.summary: Presents the Beta (effective stress) method for estimating unit shaft resistance of driven piles and drilled columns in coarse-grained or drained fine-grained soils. Covers determination of the β coefficient via earth pressure coefficient K and interface friction angle δ, step-by-step procedures, and empirical β values from multiple sources (Tables 6-13 through 6-15 and Figure 6-13).
sections.body:
The Beta method, sometimes referred to as the effective stress method, can be applied to estimate the axial capacity of deep foundations in coarse-grained soils in the short and long term as well as fine-grained soils in long-term, drained conditions. Variants of the Beta method are presented for driven piles (USACE 1991, Fellenius 2021), drilled shafts (Chen and Kulhawy 2002, FHWA 2018a), and other drilled columns (FHWA 2007, Coduto et al. 2016). Other effective stress methods, such as the Nordlund method (Nordlund 1963, 1979), can be adapted to the format of the Beta method.

The Beta method uses the coefficient, β, to relate the effective vertical stress to the unit shaft resistance. The β coefficient is found as:
β = K·tan(δ)  (6-6)
where K = earth pressure coefficient and δ = interface friction angle between the pile and the soil.

The representative unit shaft resistance (fs) is evaluated over the shaft or each segment of the shaft by:
fs = β·σ'z  (6-7)
where σ'z = average effective vertical stress over the shaft or shaft segment.

The process to find K and δ to determine β consists of evaluating 1) the at-rest earth pressure coefficient according to Jaky (1944) without adjustment for overconsolidation, based on conditions before construction, 2) the ratio of the earth pressure coefficient for the column-soil interface to the at-rest earth pressure coefficient, K/K0, 3) the effective internal friction angle, and 4) the ratio of the interface friction angle to the internal friction angle, δ/φʹ. Table 6-13 provides guidance for evaluating K/K0, and Table 6-14 provides guidance for evaluating δ/φʹ. The value of φʹ used in the analysis can be determined from laboratory testing or using empirical correlations, such as those found in Chapter 8 of DM 7.1.

The lateral earth pressure coefficient is influenced by a number of factors related to installation, such as soil displacement and disturbance from predrilling or jetting. Unless explicitly stated, the guidance provided herein does not apply to piles that are jetted, predrilled, or vibrated into place. When a pile is tapered, the perimeter changes along its length. The perimeter change can be handled directly (Nordlund 1963, 1979) or using a series of equivalent uniform segments, each having a different diameter (Fellenius 2021). Unless pile taper is handled directly (Nordlund 1963, Nordlund 1979), the value of K used should not exceed the Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient.

As an alternative to finding K and δ, the coefficient β can be evaluated directly using the empirical guidance provided in Table 6-15 or back calculated from load test results.
key_points: Beta method relates unit shaft resistance to effective vertical stress via fs = β·σ'z, where β = K·tan(δ).
K/K0 ratios differ for displacement vs. nondisplacement columns; see Figure 6-13 and Table 6-13.
Interface friction angle ratios (δ/φʹ) depend on pile material and installation method per Table 6-14.
β can be estimated directly using empirical tables (Table 6-15) as an alternative to computing K and δ separately.
Guidance does not apply to jetted, predrilled, or vibrated piles without specific adjustments.
For tapered piles not handled by the Nordlund method directly, K must not exceed the Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient.

equations.description: Beta coefficient: β = K·tan(δ), where K is the earth pressure coefficient and δ is the interface friction angle between the pile and soil.
Unit shaft resistance by Beta method: fs = β·σ'z, where σ'z is the average effective vertical stress over the shaft or shaft segment.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating shaft resistance of driven piles or drilled columns in coarse-grained soils (short or long term) or fine-grained soils under long-term drained conditions.

sections.title: Shaft Resistance for Saturated, Undrained Soils – Alpha Method
sections.summary: Presents the Alpha method for estimating unit shaft resistance in undrained (short-term) conditions for clay and silt soils. Covers multiple versions of the method including Tomlinson (1994) for driven piles, Chen et al. (2011) and Salgado (2008) for drilled shafts/CFAs, Coleman and Arcement (2002) for CFAs, and the API P2A method, with equations and curves for the adhesion factor α as a function of normalized undrained strength.
sections.body:
The Alpha method is based on an undrained characterization of shear strength and is named for the adhesion factor, α. The unit shaft resistance is also referred to as the adhesion, Cα, between the column surface and the soil. Analogous to the interface friction angle, the adhesion is related to the undrained strength by:
fs = Cα = α·su  (6-8)
where fs = unit shaft resistance and su = undrained shear strength.

Many authors have presented versions of the Alpha Method for driven piles (Tomlinson 1994, API 1993, Randolph and Murphy 1985, FHWA 2016) and for bored columns (Chen et al. 2011, Salgado 2008). In all forms of the Alpha Method, the values of α are based on empirical observations from load tests that capture installation effects and the properties of the soil-column interface. Depending on the version used, estimates of α may be sensitive to the magnitude of undrained strength, overconsolidation, normalized embedment (Z/b), pile material, installation method, and penetration of overlying soil layers. In general, disturbance of stiff clays by installation lowers adhesion and this effect becomes more pronounced as the undrained strength of the soil increases, meaning that α decreases as su increases. The value of α should be limited to values between zero and 1.0.

The effects of embedment length on α are more complex and are addressed in different ways, or ignored altogether, in different versions of the Alpha Method. For example, Tomlinson (1994) recommends reducing α due to the formation of a gap between the shaft and stiff clay near the ground surface. Normalized embedment is defined here as the distance from the ground surface to the bottom of the clay layer, sublayer, or pile, whichever comes first, divided by the pile width or diameter. The length effects described by Tomlinson (1994) are presented here; however, engineering judgment should be exercised for how to consider length effects.

The evaluation of unit shaft resistance for driven piles in clay depends in part on the consistency of the clay as described by Tomlinson (1994) and presented in Table 6-16. For piles driven into soft clay, dissipation of driving-induced pore pressures and accompanying consolidation results in adhesion that is at least as high as the undisturbed undrained strength (Tomlinson 1994), corresponding to a value of α equal to 1.0.

For driven piles in firm to very stiff clay, the relationships between α and normalized undrained strength for the Tomlinson Alpha method (Tomlinson 1994) are depicted in Figure 6-14 as Curves A and B for normalized embedments (Z/b) of 40 and 10, respectively.

Tomlinson (1994) also presents guidance to estimate α in stiff clay for special cases where the pile penetrates soft clay or sand/gravel before penetrating the stiff clay. A simple approach to account for the effects of soft clay overlying stiff clay based on Tomlinson (1994) is to define a transition zone from the top of the stiff clay along the upper length of pile in the stiff clay equal to 10 times the pile width or diameter. The value of α within this zone can be estimated by:
α = (su/Pa)^(-0.44) · 0.28  (6-9)
where su = undrained shear strength of the stiff clay layer and Pa = atmospheric pressure in same units as su.

If the calculated value of fs is lower for the transition zone than in the soft clay, the unit shaft resistance from the soft clay layer should be used for the transition zone.

Similarly, a simple approach to account for the effects of sand or gravel overlying stiff clay based on Tomlinson (1980) is to define a transition zone equal to 10 times the pile width or diameter with α = 1.0 within that zone.

For drilled shafts, Chen et al. (2011) recommends estimating α as:
α = 0.3 / (1 + 0.17·(su,ICU/Pa)) ≤ 1  (6-10)
where su,ICU = undrained strength evaluated using an ICU triaxial test and Pa = atmospheric pressure.

Values of undrained strength evaluated using UC, UU, or DSS tests can reasonably be scaled as:
su,ICU ≈ 1.74·su,UC·OCR^(-0.25)  (6-11)
su,ICU ≈ 1.68·su,UU·OCR^(-0.25)  (6-12)
su,ICU ≈ 1.43·su,DSS  (6-13)

For drilled shafts and CFAs, Salgado (2008) recommends:
α = 0.4·(1 - 0.12·ln(su/Pa))  (6-14)
for soils with a clay fraction of at least 50% and an OCR between 3 and 5.

Coleman and Arcement (2002) found:
α = (su/Pa)^0.53  (6-15)
valid for normalized strengths in the range of 0.24 to 1.42.

The P2A Method (API 1993, Randolph and Murphy 1985) calculates α as:
α = 0.5·(su/σ'z)^(-0.5) for su/σ'z ≤ 1  (6-16)
α = 0.5·(su/σ'z)^(-0.25) for su/σ'z > 1  (6-17)
When the undrained strength ratio is less than 0.25, the value of α should be capped at 1.0.

The API guidance can also be expressed in terms of OCR as:
α = 1.07·OCR^(-0.4) for OCR ≤ 4.5  (6-18)
α = 0.73·OCR^(-0.2) for OCR > 4.5  (6-19)
When the OCR is less than 1.2, the value of α should be capped at 1.0.

Codeto et al. (2016) recommend evaluating the side resistance of full-displacement DDPs in the same way as used for driven concrete displacement piles of the same nominal diameter. For partial displacement DDPs, Coduto et al. (2016) recommend interpolating side resistance somewhere between a driven concrete displacement pile and CFA pile.
key_points: Alpha method: fs = α·su, where α is an empirically derived adhesion factor ranging from 0 to 1.0.
α generally decreases as su increases due to greater disturbance of stiffer clays during installation.
Tomlinson (1994) curves A and B in Figure 6-14 apply to driven piles at Z/b ≥ 40 and Z/b = 10, respectively.
A transition zone of 10b in stiff clay underlying soft clay uses Eq. 6-9 to reduce α; underlying sand/gravel uses α = 1.0.
Chen et al. (2011) Eq. 6-10 and Salgado (2008) Eq. 6-14 are recommended for drilled shafts and CFAs.
API P2A method (Eqs. 6-16 to 6-19) uses undrained strength ratio or OCR to determine α; developed for large-diameter offshore pipe piles.
Undrained strength from UC, UU, or DSS tests can be converted to ICU-equivalent using Eqs. 6-11 to 6-13.

equations.description: Alpha method unit shaft resistance: fs = Cα = α·su, where α is the adhesion factor and su is the undrained shear strength.
Alpha factor for transition zone in stiff clay underlying soft clay: α = (su/Pa)^(-0.44) · 0.28, fit to Tomlinson (1994) curve for pile penetration 10b into stiff clay beneath soft clay.
Alpha factor for drilled shafts (Chen et al. 2011): α = 0.3 / (1 + 0.17·(su,ICU/Pa)) ≤ 1, based on ICU triaxial undrained strength.
Conversion of UC undrained strength to ICU equivalent: su,ICU ≈ 1.74·su,UC·OCR^(-0.25).
Conversion of UU undrained strength to ICU equivalent: su,ICU ≈ 1.68·su,UU·OCR^(-0.25).
Conversion of DSS undrained strength to ICU equivalent: su,ICU ≈ 1.43·su,DSS.
Alpha factor for drilled shafts and CFAs (Salgado 2008): α = 0.4·(1 - 0.12·ln(su/Pa)), for soils with clay fraction ≥ 50% and OCR between 3 and 5.
Alpha factor for CFAs in mixed alluvial/loessial deposits (Coleman and Arcement 2002): α = (su/Pa)^0.53, valid for su/Pa from 0.24 to 1.42.
API P2A method alpha factor when su/σ'z ≤ 1: α = 0.5·(su/σ'z)^(-0.5), capped at 1.0 when su/σ'z < 0.25.
API P2A method alpha factor when su/σ'z > 1: α = 0.5·(su/σ'z)^(-0.25).
API alpha method expressed in terms of OCR for OCR ≤ 4.5: α = 1.07·OCR^(-0.4).
API alpha method expressed in terms of OCR for OCR > 4.5: α = 0.73·OCR^(-0.2).

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating shaft resistance of driven piles, drilled shafts, CFAs, or DDPs in saturated, undrained (short-term) fine-grained soil conditions.

sections.title: Base Resistance
sections.summary: Introduces the considerations and limitations of applying bearing capacity theory to deep foundation base resistance. Explains why Nγ is typically eliminated, leaving only Nq for drained conditions and Nc for undrained conditions, and recommends SPT/CPT-based methods as alternatives due to limitations in predictive accuracy of theoretical approaches.
sections.body:
Given sufficient displacement for mobilization, unit base resistance, qb, is usually significantly larger for drained conditions in coarse-grained soils compared to undrained conditions in fine-grained soils. Special considerations need to be accepted and/or addressed to apply bearing capacity theory to deep foundations. These considerations include:
1) Local, or plunging, mode of failure is often more representative of bearing failure of deep foundations rather than the general shear considered by bearing capacity theory (Coduto et al. 2016).
2) The point of bearing capacity failure is usually difficult to define from the relationship of base settlement and load (Fellenius 2021).
3) Bearing capacity theory does not capture the effects of stress release and disturbance of soils below the base, particularly in drilled shafts (FHWA 2018a).
4) Bearing capacity theory does not capture the effects of adjacent elements, e.g. closely-spaced piles in the group.
5) Inputs to bearing capacity theory, e.g. friction angle, tend to have nonlinear effects on bearing capacity. Thus, small changes to inputs may have large impacts on the bearing resistance considered in design.

Due to the limitations of bearing capacity theory, Vesic (1977) states that "in most situations it may be preferable to determine pile point and skin resistances directly from field tests, such as the static (Dutch) cone test, standard penetration test, and the pressuremeter test." The SPT and CPT-based methods described in Section 6-5.4.4 are often a good alternative, particularly for coarse-grained soils.

Since the ratio of the base width to the depth below the ground surface is usually small, the Nγ term of the general bearing capacity equation is typically eliminated unless an enlarged base is used. For analysis of deep foundations in drained conditions, only the Nq term is retained. Only the Nc term is retained for short-term analysis of fine-grained soils.
key_points: Base resistance in drained coarse-grained soils is generally much larger than in undrained fine-grained soils.
Bearing capacity theory has significant limitations for deep foundations: local failure mode, difficulty defining failure, disturbance effects, group effects, and sensitivity to friction angle.
The Nγ term is typically dropped; only Nq (drained) or Nc (undrained) is retained for deep foundation analysis.
SPT/CPT-based methods are recommended as alternatives to bearing capacity theory, especially for coarse-grained soils.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the unit base resistance of any deep foundation element using bearing capacity theory, as a precursor to selecting the appropriate semi-empirical or theoretical method.

sections.title: Base Resistance for Drained Conditions – Semi-Empirical
sections.summary: Provides a semi-empirical approach to estimating drained unit base resistance using the bearing capacity factor Nq. Tabulates Nq values by soil type and friction angle from Fellenius (2021) and Cheng (2004), including an equation for Nq as a function of embedment ratio and friction angle, and applies them via Eq. 6-20 for elements with Z/b ≥ 5.
sections.body:
Estimates of the Nq factor based on the soil type and friction angle are provided in Table 6-17. The unit base resistance for deep foundation elements (Z/b ≥ 5) in drained conditions is found by:
qb = Nq·σ'zD  (6-20)
where σ'zD = vertical effective stress at the base elevation.

The equation provided in Table 6-17 is based on Cheng's (2004) correction of theory by Berezantev et al. (1961). The latter was also the basis of Nordlund's (1963, 1979) estimates of base resistance.
key_points: Unit base resistance (drained): qb = Nq·σ'zD, applicable for Z/b ≥ 5.
Nq values range widely: 3–30 for clay (φ' = 25–30°), 30–150 for sand (φ' = 32–40°), 60–300 for gravel (φ' = 35–45°) per Fellenius (2021).
Cheng (2004) provides an equation for Nq as a function of embedment ratio (Z/b) and friction angle, with a cap of 200 unless supported by project-specific data.
The Nq equation is based on Cheng's (2004) correction of Berezantev et al. (1961) theory, which also underpins the Nordlund method.

equations.description: Unit base resistance for drained conditions (Z/b ≥ 5): qb = Nq·σ'zD, where σ'zD is the vertical effective stress at the base elevation.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating unit base resistance of driven piles or drilled shafts in drained conditions with embedment ratio Z/b ≥ 5, using a semi-empirical bearing capacity factor.

sections.title: Base Resistance for Drained Conditions – Vesic
sections.summary: Presents Vesic's (1977) cavity expansion bearing capacity theory for estimating drained base resistance of driven piles. Covers the modified bearing capacity factor N*q, mean effective stress calculation, reduced rigidity index (Irr) to account for soil compressibility and local shear, and volumetric strain estimation using Boussinesq theory with Table 6-18 strain factors.
sections.body:
Vesic's (1977) bearing capacity theory for driven pile foundations is based on cavity expansion theory. Application to other deep foundation types is up to the designer's judgment. Given the tendency for local shearing, the compressibility of the soil is accounted for using modified bearing capacity factors, N*c and N*q. The unit base resistance for deep foundation elements (Z/b ≥ 5) in drained conditions is found by:
qb = N*q·σ'm  (6-21)
where σ'm = mean effective stress at b/2 below the pile base elevation.

Assuming K0 conditions, the mean effective stress is:
σ'm = (1/3)·(1 + 2·(1 - sin(φ')))·σ'zD+b/2  (6-22)
where σ'zD+b/2 = effective vertical stress at b/2 below the base prior to pile installation and φ' = peak effective friction within proximity of the base.

Vesic's method uses a reduced rigidity index (Irr) and estimates N*q by:
N*q = (e^(π·tan(φ'))·((2/3)·Irr·tan(φ')·(4·sin(φ')/(3·(1-sin(φ')))))^(...))·(...)  (6-23)
[Full formula as given in source with exponential and trigonometric terms.]

The impact of compressibility is assessed using the reduced rigidity index, Irr. The tendency for local shear failure increases as the rigidity index decreases. Characterization of the soil within 1 to 2 pile widths of the base is most important for evaluating base resistance by Vesic's bearing capacity theory.

For coarse-grained soils, the rigidity index according to Vesic (1977) is equal to:
Ir = E / (2·(1 + ν)·σ'm·tan(φ'))  (6-24)
where E = Young's Modulus and ν = Poisson's Ratio.

To account for the volume change required to mobilize shear strength, the rigidity index should be reduced to:
Irr = Ir / (1 + εv·Ir)  (6-25)
where εv = volumetric strain from the foundation loading.

For piles bearing in soil, the reduced rigidity index normally ranges from 10 to 500.

Assuming one-dimensional elastic compression below the pile, the volumetric strain can be estimated by:
εv = (1+ν)(1-2ν)/((1-ν)·Es)·∆σzD+b/2 ≈ qb,app·Fν / Es  (6-26)
where ∆σzD+b/2 = change in vertical stress at a depth of b/2 below the base, qb,app = estimated applied bearing pressure at the base of the pile, and Fν = strain factor based on Boussinesq theory and Poisson's ratio (see Table 6-18).
key_points: Vesic's method uses modified factor N*q applied to mean effective stress σ'm (not vertical stress) to account for local/plunging failure.
Mean effective stress σ'm is calculated at b/2 below the base under K0 conditions per Eq. 6-22.
The reduced rigidity index Irr accounts for soil compressibility; typical range for piles in soil is 10 to 500.
Volumetric strain εv (Eq. 6-26) is needed to compute Irr; estimated using Boussinesq theory with strain factor Fν from Table 6-18.
Vesic's theory was developed primarily for driven piles; application to other foundation types requires engineering judgment.

equations.description: Unit base resistance for drained conditions by Vesic's method (Z/b ≥ 5): qb = N*q·σ'm, where σ'm is the mean effective stress at b/2 below the pile base.
Mean effective stress at b/2 below the base assuming K0 conditions: σ'm = (1/3)·(1 + 2·(1 - sin(φ')))·σ'zD+b/2.
Vesic's (1977) modified bearing capacity factor N*q based on reduced rigidity index Irr, effective friction angle φ', incorporating cavity expansion and local shear effects.
Rigidity index for coarse-grained soils (Vesic 1977): Ir = E / (2·(1 + ν)·σ'm·tan(φ')), where E = Young's Modulus and ν = Poisson's Ratio.
Reduced rigidity index accounting for volumetric strain: Irr = Ir / (1 + εv·Ir), where εv = volumetric strain from foundation loading.
Volumetric strain estimate assuming one-dimensional elastic compression: εv = (1+ν)(1-2ν)/((1-ν)·Es)·∆σzD+b/2 ≈ qb,app·Fν / Es, where Fν is a Boussinesq-based strain factor from Table 6-18.

sections.applicability: Applies when using Vesic's (1977) cavity expansion-based bearing capacity theory to estimate drained unit base resistance for driven piles (Z/b ≥ 5), particularly where soil compressibility and local shear failure are concerns.

sections.title: Undrained Base Resistance
sections.summary: Presents methods for estimating unit base resistance of deep foundations in undrained (short-term) fine-grained soil conditions using the modified bearing capacity factor N*c. Covers Vesic's (1977) approach, Brinch Hansen's value of N*c = 9, and FHWA (1999) guidance for formed-in-place columns on weak clay using N*c as a function of rigidity index or normalized undrained strength.
sections.body:
The N*c factor is required for short-term analysis of fine-grained soils. For undrained conditions, the unit base resistance for deep foundations is:
qb = N*c·su  (6-27)
where su = undrained strength within proximity of the base.

Using Vesic's (1977) approach, the value of N*c is found by:
N*c = (4/3)·(ln(Irr) + 1) + π/2 + 1  (6-28)

For undrained conditions, the rigidity index is found by:
Irr = Ir = Eu / (3·su)  (6-29)
where Eu = Young's modulus for undrained conditions and su = undrained strength within proximity of the base.

The volume correction is not needed for undrained conditions, which involves no volume change by definition, i.e. Irr = Ir.

Methods other than Vesic (1977) are more commonly used to obtain N*c for use in Equation 6-27. According to Brinch Hansen (1957), N*c is equal to 9 based on bearing capacity theory for typical deep foundations with Z/b of at least 2.5. An exception exists for formed-in-place columns bearing on fine-grained soil having a representative undrained shear strength less than 2 ksf. In this case, interpreting the guidance by FHWA (1999) suggests that N*c is a function of Ir:
N*c = 1.33·(ln(Ir) + 1) ≤ 9  (6-30)
or a function of normalized undrained shear strength:
N*c = 10.2 - 12.4·(su/Pa) / (0.1 + su/Pa) ≤ 9  (6-31)

Unlike piles bearing in coarse-grained soils, bearing resistance in clay is often not the dominant contributor to the total nominal axial resistance.
key_points: Undrained unit base resistance: qb = N*c·su (Eq. 6-27).
Brinch Hansen (1957) recommends N*c = 9 for Z/b ≥ 2.5, which is the most commonly used value.
For formed-in-place columns on weak clay (su < 2 ksf), N*c may be less than 9 and is a function of Ir (Eq. 6-30) or normalized su (Eq. 6-31).
For undrained conditions, Irr = Ir = Eu/(3·su); no volumetric strain correction is needed.
Bearing resistance in clay is often not the dominant component of total axial resistance.

equations.description: Undrained unit base resistance for deep foundations: qb = N*c·su, where su is the undrained strength within proximity of the base.
Vesic's (1977) N*c factor for undrained base resistance: N*c = (4/3)·(ln(Irr) + 1) + π/2 + 1.
Rigidity index for undrained conditions: Irr = Ir = Eu / (3·su), where Eu = undrained Young's modulus.
N*c as a function of rigidity index for formed-in-place columns on weak clay (FHWA 1999): N*c = 1.33·(ln(Ir) + 1) ≤ 9.
N*c as a function of normalized undrained shear strength for formed-in-place columns on weak clay (FHWA 1999): N*c = 10.2 - 12.4·(su/Pa) / (0.1 + su/Pa) ≤ 9.

sections.applicability: Applies when estimating base resistance of deep foundations bearing in saturated fine-grained soils under short-term, undrained loading conditions.

sections.title: SPT and CPT-based SCA Methods
sections.summary: Presents empirical SPT- and CPT-based methods for estimating shaft friction and base resistance of deep foundations, as alternatives to Beta/Alpha methods. Covers the LCPC method (Bustamante and Gianeselli 1982) for CPT-based unit side and base resistance, with equations and tables for side resistance factor ks, maximum unit side resistance fp, and base bearing factor kt for four foundation type groups.
sections.body:
Many published methods empirically relate shaft and base resistance to the resistances measured by the SPT and CPT (Poulos 1989, Fellenius 2021). In many instances, SPT and CPT-based estimates of base resistance are used in conjunction with estimates of shaft resistance by the Beta and/or Alpha methods. Additionally, certain foundation technologies, such as DDPs, have not yet reached a state of maturity where specific versions of the Beta and Alpha method are available, and presently, designers must rely on SPT and CPT-based SCA methods.

Other in situ tests, such as the dilatometer or pressuremeter, can also be used to evaluate axial capacity (Fellenius 2021, Briaud 2013). Presentation of pressuremeter and dilatometer-based methods are beyond the scope of this chapter.

Table 6-19 lists selected methods for estimating shaft friction using SPT blow count, and Table 6-20 lists selected methods for estimating base resistance.

CPT results can also be used to estimate the static axial capacity of deep foundations. The empirical approach developed by the Laboratoire Central des Points et Chausses (LCPC) (Bustamante and Gianesselli, 1982) is presented here due to its simplicity and adaptability to a range of deep foundation technologies.

Nominal unit side resistance and unit base resistance are estimated according to the LCPC method as:
fs/Pa = (1/ks)·(qc/Pa) ≤ fp/Pa  (6-32)
and
qb/Pa = kt·(qc,a/Pa)  (6-33)
where qc/Pa = cone tip resistance normalized by atmospheric pressure, qc,a/Pa = average normalized cone tip resistance in the vicinity of the base, ks = side resistance factor (see Table 6-21), fp = maximum unit side resistance (see Table 6-22), and kt = base bearing factor (see Table 6-23).

The average cone tip resistance in the vicinity of the base is found by averaging resistance values over 1.5·b above and below the base. Values above the base should be discarded until all values fall within 70% to 130% of the average value. Likewise, values below the base should be discarded until all values do not exceed 130% of the average value.

Values of ks, fp, and kt are found using Table 6-21, Table 6-22, and Table 6-23, respectively, based on the categorization of the foundation type and soil conditions. Foundations falling under Group I-A include drilled shafts without permanent casing, CFAs, gravity-grouted micropiles, and barrettes. Group I-B foundations include drilled shafts with permanent casing. Group II-A foundations include driven and jacked concrete piles. Group II-B foundations include driven and jacked steel piles.
key_points: SPT-based shaft and base resistance methods (Table 6-19, Table 6-20) are commonly used alongside Beta/Alpha methods and are essential for DDPs.
LCPC (CPT-based) method: unit side resistance fs/Pa = (qc/Pa)/ks ≤ fp/Pa; unit base resistance qb/Pa = kt·(qc,a/Pa).
Average qc,a for base resistance is computed over 1.5b above and below the base with outlier exclusion criteria.
Foundation types classified into Groups I-A, I-B, II-A, II-B; each group has different ks, fp, and kt values.
Pressuremeter and dilatometer methods exist but are beyond the scope of this chapter.
SPT methods from Meyerhof, Brown, Briaud, and NeSmith cover driven piles, drilled shafts, CFAs, and DDPs.

equations.description: LCPC CPT-based nominal unit side resistance: fs/Pa = (qc/Pa)/ks ≤ fp/Pa, where ks is the side resistance factor and fp is the maximum unit side resistance.
LCPC CPT-based nominal unit base resistance: qb/Pa = kt·(qc,a/Pa), where kt is the base bearing factor and qc,a is the average cone tip resistance in the vicinity of the base.

sections.applicability: Applies when using SPT blow counts or CPT cone tip resistance to empirically estimate shaft friction and base resistance for driven piles, drilled shafts, CFAs, and DDPs, particularly when Beta/Alpha methods are unavailable or supplementary field-test-based estimates are desired.

sections.title: Micropiles
sections.summary: Covers axial capacity estimation for micropiles in direct load support applications. Micropiles develop capacity almost entirely through side resistance in the bond zone. Presents Eq. 6-34 for nominal side resistance using unit grout-to-ground bond strength, with Table 6-24 providing preliminary bond strength estimates by soil/rock type and grouting method (Types A–D). Notes that structural capacity often governs.
sections.body:
Guidance for micropiles used in direct load support applications is provided in FHWA (2005). Due to their small diameter, micropiles develop axial capacity primarily through side resistance developed between the grout and the soil and/or rock in the bond zone. Base resistance is usually neglected; however, for micropiles terminating within hard rock, the procedures for evaluating the base resistance of rock-socketed drilled shafts, described in Section 6-5.4.6.2, can be applied. Given the possibility of high grout-to-ground bond strength, structural capacity often limits micropile capacity.

The nominal side resistance of a micropile bonded in soil or rock can be estimated using:
Rs = αbond·π·b·Zb  (6-34)
where αbond = nominal unit grout-to-ground bond strength, b = diameter of the bond zone, and Zb = length of the bond zone.

Table 6-24 can be used to make preliminary estimates of αbond, which is sensitive to the grout mix, grout delivery method, and soil/rock properties. Load testing and local experience is most often used to evaluate nominal unit side resistance.
